```{r setup}
library(mixvlmc)
```

This vignette covers two complementary aspects of `mixvlmc`: the
representation of the discrete time series used to estimate models, and the
detailed exploration of the contexts of fitted models. It assumes some
familiarity with the notions introduced in `vignette("context-trees")`
(contexts, context trees, `contexts()` with `frequency`, and the basic node
functions `find_sequence()`, `is_context()`, `children()`, `counts()` and
`positions()`), in `vignette("variable-length-markov-chains")` and in
`vignette("covlmc")`.

## Discrete time series

### Creating a discrete time series

Since version 0.3.0, `mixvlmc` represents discrete time series by objects of
class `dts`, created by the `dts()` function. A `dts` stores the time series
together with its _state space_, i.e. the set of values that the series can
take. A `dts` can be built from a numeric, character, factor or logical vector.
When the state space is not specified, it is computed from the vector in a way
that depends on its type. For numeric and character vectors, the state space
consists of the unique values of the series, in increasing order:

```{r}
x_num <- dts(c(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3))
x_num
states(x_num)
x_chr <- dts(c("b", "a", "c", "a", "b"))
states(x_chr)
```

For a factor, the state space is given by the levels of the factor, including
levels that do not appear in the series, and in the order of the levels:

```{r}
x_fct <- dts(factor(c("low", "high", "low"),
  levels = c("low", "medium", "high")
))
x_fct
```

For a logical vector, the state space is always `c(FALSE, TRUE)`:

```{r}
x_lgl <- dts(c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE))
states(x_lgl)
```

By default, only the first 5 values of the series are printed, but this can be
changed with the `n` parameter of `print()`:

```{r}
set.seed(0)
x_long <- dts(sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 50, replace = TRUE))
x_long
print(x_long, n = 15)
```

`is_dts()` tests whether an object is a discrete time series, `states()`
returns its state space and `dts_data()` recovers the original series as a
vector (of the same type as the state space):

```{r}
is_dts(x_chr)
is_dts(c("b", "a", "c"))
dts_data(x_chr)
dts_data(x_fct)
```

The length of a `dts` is given by `length()` and a `dts` can be subsetted with
`[`. The result is a `dts` with the same state space, even if some states do
not appear in the subset:

```{r}
length(x_long)
x_long[1:2]
```

Discrete time series cannot contain missing values:

```{r}
try(dts(c("a", NA, "b")))
```

### Specifying the state space

The state space can be given explicitly with the `vals` parameter of `dts()`.
This has two uses. First, it sets the order of the states, which is the order
used by all the functions of the package (for instance to order the columns of
the results of `contexts()` or `predict()`, or the probabilities displayed by
`draw()`). Second, the state space can include states that do not appear in
the series:

```{r}
x_abc <- dts(c("b", "a", "b"), vals = c("c", "b", "a"))
x_abc
```

When `vals` is given, `dts()` checks that the series only contains values of
the state space:

```{r}
try(dts(c("a", "d"), vals = c("a", "b", "c")))
```

### Why use a discrete time series object?

All the estimation functions of the package (`ctx_tree()`, `vlmc()`,
`covlmc()`, `tune_vlmc()` and `tune_covlmc()`) accept either a plain vector or
a `dts`. In the former case, the vector is converted with `dts()` using the
default state space. Using a `dts` directly is useful mainly when the state
space of the model cannot be deduced reliably from the series used to
estimate it, a common situation when several series are analysed with the same
state space.

Let us consider the household electricity consumption data set
`powerconsumption`. As in `vignette("covlmc")`, the active power is discretised
into three levels. The following function extracts the discretised series of
some weeks of the data set (as a character vector):

```{r}
power_levels <- c("low", "typical", "high")
power_weeks <- function(weeks) {
  pc <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week %in% weeks, ]
  as.character(cut(pc$active_power,
    breaks = c(0, 0.4, 2, 8),
    labels = power_levels
  ))
}
week_33 <- power_weeks(33)
week_35 <- power_weeks(35)
table(week_33)
table(week_35)
```

The consumption is very low during week 33, in August (probably because of
holidays), and the `high` level is never observed. A model estimated on this
week from the character vector has therefore only two states and it cannot be
used on week 35:

```{r}
model_33_raw <- vlmc(week_33)
states(model_33_raw)
try(loglikelihood(model_33_raw, newdata = week_35))
```

If we specify the state space with a `dts`, the model knows that the `high`
level exists:

```{r}
week_33_dts <- dts(week_33, vals = power_levels)
model_33 <- vlmc(week_33_dts)
model_33
loglikelihood(model_33, newdata = week_35)
```

The log likelihood is now computed, and its value, $-\infty$, tells us that
week 35 is impossible according to the model of week 33, as the `high` level
was never observed during that week. The predicted probabilities include all
the states of the state space, in the specified order (the last row is the
prediction of the state that follows the series, see `predict.vlmc()`):

```{r}
predict(model_33, newdata = week_35[1:5], type = "probs")
```

Notice that the new data (`newdata` in `loglikelihood()` and `predict()`, `init`
in `simulate()` or the sequence given to `find_sequence()`) can be given as a
plain vector or as a `dts`. In both cases, it is interpreted in the state space
of the model: a `dts` with a different state space is accepted provided its
values belong to the state space of the model. For instance, the following call
computes the log likelihood of week 34, in which the `high` level is also
absent, with the model of week 33:

```{r}
week_34_dts <- dts(power_weeks(34))
states(week_34_dts)
loglikelihood(model_33, newdata = week_34_dts)
```

When the series is a factor, its levels define the state space, so
discretising directly with `cut()` (without the conversion to character used
above) also gives a model with three states:

```{r}
states(vlmc(factor(week_33, levels = power_levels)))
```

Finally, `simulate()` does not return a `dts` but a vector of the same type as
the state space of the model (here a character vector), whose values are taken
from this state space. It can be converted into a `dts` with the same state
space as follows:

```{r}
sim_33 <- simulate(model_33, 20, seed = 0)
sim_33
dts(sim_33, vals = states(model_33))
```

## Contexts of a VLMC

In the rest of this vignette, we use a VLMC estimated on week 5 of the
electricity consumption data set. We keep the positions of the contexts in the
time series with `keep_match = TRUE` (they are not kept by default). The model
is estimated with the default C++ backend (see `vlmc()`), but all the functions
described below work in the same way with the R backend (`backend = "R"`).

```{r}
week_5 <- dts(power_weeks(5), vals = power_levels)
model_5 <- vlmc(week_5, keep_match = TRUE)
model_5
draw(model_5)
```

### Two representations

`contexts()` gives two representations of the contexts of a model. By
default, it returns a list of `ctx_node` objects, one per context, which can
be explored with the node functions described in the next section:

```{r}
ctxs_5 <- contexts(model_5)
ctxs_5
```

With `sequence = TRUE`, or as soon as additional information is requested
(see below), the function returns a data frame with one row per context. Its
first column, `context`, is a list: each element is a vector of states (of the
same type as `states(model_5)`) that represents a context. As the default
printing of such a column is truncated, we define a small helper function that
replaces each context by a character string, only for display purposes:

```{r}
flat_contexts <- function(ctx_df) {
  ctx_df$context <- vapply(ctx_df$context, paste, character(1), collapse = ", ")
  ctx_df
}
ctx_df_5 <- contexts(model_5, sequence = TRUE)
ctx_df_5$context[[1]]
```

Contexts are written by default in temporal order (the most recent state is on
the right), while `reverse = TRUE` uses the reverse order of Bühlmann and Wyner
(the most recent state is on the left), which corresponds to the paths from the
root in the representation of `draw()`:

```{r}
head(flat_contexts(contexts(model_5, sequence = TRUE, reverse = TRUE)))
```

The parameter `reverse` has the same effect on the list representation and can
also be given to the `print()` function of a list of contexts
(`print(ctxs_5, reverse = TRUE)`).

The additional columns depend on the parameters of `contexts()` and on the
class of the model, as summarised below (`contexts()` accepts the same
parameters for both backends of `ctx_tree()` and `vlmc()`, but the order of the
contexts may differ from one backend to the other).

| parameter | `ctx_tree` | `vlmc` | `covlmc` | columns |
|-----------|:----------:|:------:|:--------:|---------|
| `frequency` | yes | yes | yes | `freq`, one per state if `"detailed"` |
| `positions` | yes | yes | yes | `positions` |
| `local` | no | yes | yes | (modifies the counts) |
| `cutoff` | no | yes | no | `cutoff` |
| `metrics` | no | yes | yes | `accuracy`, `auc` |
| `model` | no | no | yes | `coef` or `model` |
| `hsize` | no | no | yes | `hsize` |
| `merging` | no | no | yes | `merged` |

### Counts

As for context trees, `frequency = "total"` adds a `freq` column with the
number of occurrences of each context in the time series (not including a
possible final occurrence not followed by any state), while
`frequency = "detailed"` adds in addition one column per state with the number
of times the context is followed by this state:

```{r}
flat_contexts(contexts(model_5, frequency = "detailed"))
```

These counts are the ones used to estimate the transition probabilities of the
model shown by `draw()`: for instance, the probabilities associated with the
context `low` are obtained by dividing the counts of the `low` row by its
`freq` value.

In a VLMC, a context can be the suffix of longer contexts. For instance,
`high, high` is the last part of `high, high, high`. The counts above include
all the occurrences of `high, high`, including the ones that are the last part
of an occurrence of `high, high, high`. With `local = TRUE`, the counts
include only the occurrences of the context that are not the last part of a
longer context, that is the time steps at which the context is the one actually
used by the model to predict the next state:

```{r}
ctx_local_5 <- contexts(model_5, frequency = "detailed", local = TRUE)
flat_contexts(ctx_local_5)
```

Each time step is associated with at most one context, so that the sum of the
local counts, `r sum(ctx_local_5$freq)`, is smaller than the length of the time
series, `r length(week_5)` (the first time steps do not have a long enough past
and the last state is not followed by any state). Some contexts have zero local
counts. For instance, the context `high` exists only because the model must
define a next state distribution after the sequence `low, high`, which never
appears in the time series: the context `high` is used only for this
unobserved sequence, while all the actual occurrences of `high` are covered by
longer contexts.

### Cut off values

For a VLMC, `cutoff` adds a `cutoff` column that summarises, for each
context, the likelihood ratio test that compares the next state distribution of
the context with the one of its parent, the context obtained by removing its
oldest state. With `cutoff = "native"` the value is the log likelihood ratio,
while `cutoff = "quantile"` gives it in the quantile scale (the p-value of the
test). See `cutoff()`, `prune()`, `vignette("variable-length-markov-chains")`
and `vignette("model-selection")` for details on these two scales.

```{r}
flat_contexts(contexts(model_5, cutoff = "quantile"))
```

The model was estimated with the default `alpha = 0.05` and a context with a
quantile value lower than `alpha` is significantly different from its parent.
Some contexts have larger values: they are kept in the model because one of
their descendants in the context tree is significant (for instance a context
`low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low` is kept because its extension `typical,
low, low, low, low, low, low, low, low` is significant). Notice that those
values are not those reported by `cutoff(model_5)` (see the dedicated section
in the documentation of `contexts.vlmc()`).

### Predictive metrics

With `metrics = TRUE`, `contexts()` adds predictive quality metrics for each
context, computed on the time steps at which the context is used by the model
(i.e. the ones counted by `local = TRUE`):

```{r}
flat_contexts(contexts(model_5,
  frequency = "total", local = TRUE,
  metrics = TRUE
))
```

The `accuracy` column gives the proportion of those time steps at which the
most probable state according to the context is the observed next state (it is
not defined when the local count is zero). For a VLMC, the predicted
probabilities are identical for all the time steps of a context: the `auc`
column is therefore not informative (it is either 0.5 or missing when some
states never follow the context). It is more useful for a VLMC with covariates,
see below. The metrics of the whole model are given by `metrics(model_5)` (see
`vignette("prediction")`).

### Positions

With `positions = TRUE`, a `positions` column gives for each context the list
of its positions in the time series. A position of a context is the index $t$
of its last state, so that $x_{t+1}$ is the state that follows the context.
Positions are available only if they have been kept during the estimation
(`keep_match = TRUE` for `vlmc()`, `keep_position = TRUE`, the default, for
`ctx_tree()`, always for `covlmc()`). As the positions are numerous, the column
is better explored programmatically:

```{r}
ctx_pos_5 <- contexts(model_5, frequency = "total", positions = TRUE)
head(ctx_pos_5$positions[[1]])
```

Positions cover all the occurrences of a context, not only the local ones.
Unlike the counts, they include a possible final occurrence of the context, at
the end of the time series, which is not followed by any state. Here the series
ends with a sequence of `low` states, so the last time step,
`r length(week_5)`, is a position of several contexts, which have therefore one
more position than their count:

```{r}
at_end <- sapply(ctx_pos_5$positions, function(pos) length(week_5) %in% pos)
ctx_pos_end <- flat_contexts(ctx_pos_5[at_end, c("context", "freq")])
ctx_pos_end$nb_positions <- lengths(ctx_pos_5$positions[at_end])
ctx_pos_end
```

## Contexts of a VLMC with covariates

We use now the data of `vignette("covlmc")`: weeks 15 and 16 of the
electricity consumption data set, with a covariate that indicates whether the
observation is made during the day or during the night.

```{r}
elec_dts <- dts(power_weeks(c(15, 16)), vals = power_levels)
pc_15_16 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week %in% c(15, 16), ]
elec_cov <- data.frame(day = (pc_15_16$hour >= 7 & pc_15_16$hour <= 18))
elec_model <- covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov)
elec_model
draw(elec_model)
```

`contexts()` supports for COVLMC the `frequency`, `local`, `positions` and
`metrics` parameters with the same meaning as for a VLMC. As the transition
probabilities of a COVLMC depend on the covariates, the `auc` column is now
informative: for a context whose model uses the covariates, it measures how
well the probabilities computed by its model separate the possible next states.
The parameter `hsize` adds a column that gives the number of past values of the
covariates used by the model of each context (0 for a context whose model does
not use the covariates).

```{r}
flat_contexts(contexts(elec_model,
  frequency = "detailed", hsize = TRUE,
  metrics = TRUE
))
```

The models themselves can be included in the data frame, either as their
coefficients (`model = "coef"`) or as the R objects produced by the estimation
engine (`model = "full"`, see `covlmc()` and the article [Computing engines and
control of VLMC with
covariates](https://fabrice-rossi.github.io/mixvlmc/articles/covlmc-engines.html)
for details about the engines). As for contexts, the corresponding column is a
list:

```{r}
ctx_coef <- contexts(elec_model, model = "coef")
ctx_coef$coef[[1]]
```

Finally, when the state space has at least three states, some contexts of a
COVLMC can be _merged_: they share a single model. This happens for instance
with a stricter cut off:

```{r}
elec_model_merged <- covlmc(elec_dts, elec_cov, alpha = 1e-7)
draw(elec_model_merged)
```

In this representation (see the article [Drawing context trees and
models](https://fabrice-rossi.github.io/mixvlmc/articles/drawing.html)), the
leaf `low, high` denotes the two merged contexts `low, typical` and
`high, typical`. `contexts()` reports merged contexts individually;
`merging = TRUE` adds a `merged` column that identifies them:

```{r}
flat_contexts(contexts(elec_model_merged,
  frequency = "total", merging = TRUE,
  metrics = TRUE
))
```

As merged contexts share their model, they share also their metrics, computed
on all the time steps of the merged contexts.

## Navigating the contexts of a fitted model

### Nodes of a VLMC

The function `find_sequence()` described in `vignette("context-trees")` also
applies to fitted models. It returns `NULL` when the sequence is not
represented in the context tree of the model:

```{r}
find_sequence(model_5, c("low", "high"))
```

and a `ctx_node` object otherwise. Such a node can be a context or not:

```{r}
node_typical <- find_sequence(model_5, "typical")
node_typical
is_context(node_typical)
node_th <- find_sequence(model_5, c("typical", "high"))
node_th
is_context(node_th)
```

The sequence represented by a node is obtained with `as_sequence()`. Its order
(temporal or reverse) is the one used to create the node (by `find_sequence()`
or `contexts()`), as reported by `is_reversed()`, and can be switched with
`rev()` or overridden with the `reverse` parameter of `as_sequence()`:

```{r}
as_sequence(node_th)
is_reversed(node_th)
node_th_rev <- rev(node_th)
node_th_rev
as_sequence(node_th_rev)
as_sequence(node_th_rev, reverse = FALSE)
```

The context tree can be traversed with `parent()`, which removes the oldest
state of the sequence (it returns `NULL` for the root of the tree, the empty
sequence), and `children()`, which returns a list with one element per state
(`NULL` when the corresponding extension of the sequence is not in the tree):

```{r}
parent(node_th)
parent(parent(node_th))
children(node_th)
```

The `counts()` function supports the `local` parameter, as `contexts()`:

```{r}
counts(node_th)
counts(node_th, local = TRUE)
```

The positions of the node in the time series are given by `positions()`. As
the state that follows a context at position $t$ is $x_{t+1}$, the counts can
be recovered from the positions and the original series (a final occurrence at
the end of the series would give a missing value, ignored by `table()`):

```{r}
pos_th <- positions(node_th)
head(pos_th)
table(factor(dts_data(week_5)[pos_th + 1], levels = power_levels))
```

Finally, `cutoff()` and `metrics()` give, for a single context, the
information reported by the corresponding parameters of `contexts()`. Notice
that `cutoff()` uses by default the quantile scale and modifies slightly the
value to ensure that the context is pruned when the value is used in
`prune()` (use `raw = TRUE` to get the exact value, see `cutoff.ctx_node()`):

```{r}
cutoff(node_th)
cutoff(node_th, scale = "native", raw = TRUE)
metrics(node_th)
```

`metrics()` can only be applied to contexts:

```{r}
try(metrics(node_typical))
```

### Nodes of a VLMC with covariates

For a COVLMC, `find_sequence()` and `contexts()` return `ctx_node_covlmc`
objects. In addition to the functions described above, `model()` gives the
model of a context, either as its coefficients (by default) or as the full
model, while `covariate_memory()` gives the number of past values of the
covariates used by this model (as the `hsize` column of `contexts()`):

```{r}
node_low <- find_sequence(elec_model, "low")
node_low
model(node_low)
model(node_low, type = "full")
covariate_memory(node_low)
metrics(node_low)
```

Both functions return `NULL` for a node that is not a context:

```{r}
node_tt <- find_sequence(elec_model, c("typical", "typical"))
is_context(node_tt)
model(node_tt)
covariate_memory(node_tt)
```

`is_merged()` tells whether a context is merged with other contexts and
`merged_with()` returns them (as a list with one element per state, in the
same way as `children()`: the merged contexts differ only in their oldest
state):

```{r}
ctxs_merged <- contexts(elec_model_merged)
sapply(ctxs_merged, is_merged)
node_lt <- find_sequence(elec_model_merged, c("low", "typical"))
merged_with(node_lt)
identical(model(node_lt), model(merged_with(node_lt)$high))
merged_with(find_sequence(elec_model_merged, "low"))
```

## Worked examples

### Predictable contexts and when they occur

Using the node functions, we can easily compute summary information about the
contexts of a VLMC. The following function gives, for a context, its length,
the most probable next state with its probability and the number of time steps
at which the context is used by the model:

```{r}
context_summary <- function(node) {
  freqs <- counts(node)
  probs <- unlist(freqs[, -1]) / freqs$total
  data.frame(
    context = paste(as_sequence(node), collapse = ", "),
    length = length(as_sequence(node)),
    next_state = names(probs)[which.max(probs)],
    probability = max(probs),
    usage = counts(node, frequency = "total", local = TRUE)
  )
}
summary_5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(contexts(model_5), context_summary))
```

We look for the contexts whose next state is almost deterministic (with a
probability of at least 0.9) and that are actually used, ordered by
decreasing length:

```{r}
predictable <- summary_5[summary_5$probability >= 0.9 & summary_5$usage > 0, ]
predictable[order(predictable$length, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Long sequences of the `low` level are likely to be followed by another `low`
observation. The positions of the corresponding contexts can be related to
other information available in the data set, for instance the hour of the
day. Let us consider the longest context made only of `low` states:

```{r}
all_low <- function(node) all(as_sequence(node) == "low")
low_ctxs <- Filter(all_low, contexts(model_5))
low_lengths <- sapply(low_ctxs, function(node) length(as_sequence(node)))
longest_low <- low_ctxs[[which.max(low_lengths)]]
longest_low
pc_5 <- powerconsumption[powerconsumption$week == 5, ]
table(hour = pc_5$hour[positions(longest_low)])
```

As expected, those long periods of low consumption happen mostly during the
night and the early morning.

### Contexts that use the covariates

In a COVLMC, the dependency of the transition probabilities on the covariates
is context specific. The contexts that actually use the covariates are
obtained as follows:

```{r}
uses_covariate <- function(node) covariate_memory(node) > 0
uses_cov <- Filter(uses_covariate, contexts(elec_model))
uses_cov
```

To understand the effect of the covariate, we can for instance compare the
empirical distribution of the next state during the day and during the night,
using the positions of each context (the value of the covariate at the
position of a context is the most recent one available to its model):

```{r}
next_state_by_day <- function(node) {
  pos <- positions(node)
  ## remove a possible final occurrence
  pos <- pos[pos < length(elec_dts)]
  prop.table(table(
    day = elec_cov$day[pos],
    next_state = factor(dts_data(elec_dts)[pos + 1], levels = power_levels)
  ), margin = 1)
}
next_state_by_day(uses_cov[[1]])
```

After a `low` observation, the next observation is more likely to stay `low`
at night than during the day. The comparison with a context whose model does
not use the covariate shows smaller differences:

```{r}
next_state_by_day(find_sequence(elec_model, "high"))
```

Finally, the predictive metrics of the contexts that use the covariates show
that their AUC is larger than 0.5, the value obtained by a context whose
predictions do not depend on the covariates (see the `auc` column above):

```{r}
sapply(uses_cov, function(node) unlist(metrics(node)[c("accuracy", "auc")]))
```
